in_english.name: Mahshid
in_english.long_meaning: Mahshid is derived from the Arabic root (m-sh-d), which means to plan, prepare, and organize. In Islamic tradition, Mahshid is associated with the concept of justice, fairness, and compassion. It is also linked to the idea of achieving spiritual growth and self-improvement through one's actions and deeds.

historical_references.context: Mahshid bint Amr ibn al-As was the wife of the Umayyad Caliph Muawiya I. She is described as a 'lady of great beauty and wisdom'. Mahshid played a pivotal role in the negotiations between Muawiya and Constantine III, the Byzantine Emperor, that led to the peace treaty between the two powers. This treaty allowed Muslims to trade freely in the Byzantine territories and facilitated the spread of Islam in Syria and beyond.

historical_references.context: Mahshid bint Marwan al-Khazraj was a prominent poetess and a descendant of the Khazraj tribe in Medina. She is famously known for her panegyric poem, 'Lamiyyat Mahshid', composed in honor of Caliph al-Mansur. This poem is regarded as one of the finest examples of classical Arabic poetry and reflects the culture and values of the Abbasid Caliphate.
